title: TRVs in heat pump systems: why they behave differently and how to set them
subtitle: Setting thermostatic radiator valves correctly when the heat source is a heat pump, not a boiler
excerpt: The thermostatic radiator valves fitted to gas-boiler radiators are designed for high-flow-temperature systems. A heat pump runs at 35 to 45°C flow, not 70 to 80°C, and needs a different approach to TRV use. Closing TRVs in unused rooms forces the flow temperature up to overcome the increased pressure, reducing heat pump efficiency. Understanding how to set TRVs for a heat pump system avoids this common problem.
sourceNotes: Heat Pump Association UK best practice guide for TRV settings 2024. Energy Saving Trust radiator and TRV guidance for heat pump systems. Ground Source Heat Pump Association (GSHPA) Technical Standards.

glossaryTerms.definition: Thermostatic Radiator Valve. A valve fitted to a radiator that opens and closes in response to room temperature, reducing flow when the room is warm and opening fully when it is cold.

The temperature of the water entering the radiator from the heat pump. A heat pump runs at 35–45°C flow; a gas boiler runs at 65–75°C. For the same heat output, a lower flow temperature requires a larger radiator surface.
A valve that opens to allow water to circulate when all TRVs are closed. Required in any central heating system with TRVs to prevent the circulating pump running against a closed circuit.

content.text: A gas boiler forces hot water at 70 to 75°C through radiators. The high temperature means a relatively small radiator area provides the required heat output, and closing a few TRVs has little effect on the system pressure or flow rate. A heat pump circulates water at 35 to 45°C, often less than half the temperature. The same radiator at
of 40°C gives roughly 40% of the heat output it gives at 75°C. This means the whole radiator area in the house is needed, closing
in spare rooms significantly reduces the total emitter surface and forces the heat pump to compensate.
The pressure problem with closed TRVs

When TRVs close, the hydraulic resistance of the circuit increases. In a gas boiler system, the boiler modulates the flow rate and the effect is modest. In a heat pump system, many units are designed to maintain a minimum flow rate, they will increase the circulating pump speed and raise the flow temperature to overcome the resistance. Both actions reduce efficiency: the pump uses more electricity and the higher flow temperature reduces the heat pump's COP. The compressor runs harder to achieve what better-distributed flow would provide cheaply.
How to set TRVs in a heat pump system
Open all TRVs fully in rooms that are being heated. The heat pump heats all rooms to the setpoint; the living space thermostat controls when the system turns off, not the TRVs.

For permanently unused rooms (a spare bedroom), set the TRV to the lowest frost-protection setting (usually star or 1) rather than closing it fully. This maintains a small flow and reduces the hydraulic resistance spike.

Consider replacing standard TRVs with lower-temperature head types rated for 35 to 45°C systems. Standard TRVs have a temperature range of around 7 to 28°C, which is compatible with heat pump flow temperatures, but the head calibration may not be optimised for it. Ask your heat pump installer to confirm compatibility.

Radiators designed for a gas boiler at 70°C flow may be too small for a heat pump at 40°C flow. A radiator producing 1,500 W at 70°C gives roughly 640 W at 40°C, less than half. If a room stays cold, fitting a larger or second radiator is often the right fix rather than raising the flow temperature. Your MCS installer should have done a room-by-room sizing check at design; ask for that document.
